title: What Your Battery Cannot Say
scopeNote: This keeps the constrained selection and the two-part verdict. The constraint is the mechanism: without a binding budget every question gets answered and there is nothing to learn. Two further referrals with different questions, seven more task types, and the battery-against-battery comparison stay in the longer version.
summary: One fictional referral, eight questions it raises, ten tasks and eighty minutes. Full coverage needs ninety, so every battery leaves something open, and the report says what.
learningObjectives: Treat a battery as a set of choices about what not to find out.
Identify which questions a given selection leaves open.
Explain why a report listing only conclusions invites the reader to assume the rest was normal.
Recognise mood, sleep and recent illness as the coverage most often squeezed out.
Explain why an engagement check matters for someone who attended reluctantly.
interactionTypes: a constrained selection under a binding time budget
a refusal, with a reason, when a task would exceed the budget
a verdict in two equally weighted halves
feedback that differs by which questions were left open
privacy: Nothing is collected, stored or transmitted.
accessibilityNotes: Keyboard operable throughout, with every task a labelled checkbox stating its duration and what it speaks to, so the trade-off is legible without any chart. A task that would exceed the budget is refused with a spoken reason rather than silently ignored, and the checkbox is returned to its previous state. Time used and questions covered are live counters with their remainders stated in words. The verdict is two lists in two cards of equal weight, headed in words, so what the battery cannot say is not visually subordinate to what it can. Every stage is announced through a polite live region.
dataStatus: A fictional referral and invented task durations. Nothing here is a real test, protocol or patient.
simulationNotes: The budget is eighty minutes and the durations are set so that full coverage needs ninety, which is verified exhaustively over all 1024 selections in the test suite. An earlier draft allowed all eight questions to be covered in 59 of 90 minutes, which made the activity's premise false and would have left the cannot panel empty; the constraint has to bite or there is nothing to learn. The best coverage achievable within budget is seven of eight, using seventy minutes, and the question that has to be dropped in that selection is new learning, which is the one the referral is actually about. Mood, sleep and recent illness are on the question list deliberately and are individually cheap, because they are what gets squeezed out and they are what could account for the whole picture without any progressive condition.
readmeTopic: why the useful half of an assessment report is the list of what was not assessed
